title: When something breaks and you don't understand the error
promise: You'll know how to find the real error message and copy it in full. With it you'll build a six-point report. That report gets the AI to fix the bug in one or two rounds, instead of rewriting your project blind.
why: Nacho is a physical therapist in Gijon and built a page with Claude so his patients could book appointments without calling him. It worked on his computer. He published it, opened it on his phone, and got a blank white screen, with not a single message explaining anything. He wrote "it doesn't work" and in three hours went through five complete rewrites that left the page worse than at the start. The message that explained everything had been there since minute one, in a browser panel Nacho didn't know existed. It named, exactly, which file was missing.

theory.title: The AI wrote the code, but it's never seen it run
theory.text: You ask Claude or ChatGPT for a page. It writes the code (the instructions the computer reads and executes) and hands it to you. That's where its involvement ends. What runs that code is your browser, on your computer, with your files, your connection, and your version of Windows. Of all that, the AI receives nothing: no image, no notice, no beep. It's the doubt everyone has the first time: if it wrote it, how doesn't it know what's wrong? The answer is that writing and running are two different things, and they happen in two different places. You're its only sensor: whatever you tell it is, literally, everything it's going to know about the failure. And "it doesn't work" carries the same information as "hello." When you don't give it data, the AI doesn't sit still waiting: it guesses, and guessing here means rewriting pieces that were perfectly fine.
theory.analogy: It's an architect who mailed you the blueprints. He knows exactly what he drew, but he's not on site. He can't know the bricklayer hung the door backwards until someone tells him. And if you just say "the house is wrong," he redesigns the whole floor plan.
theory.example: Nacho wrote "the page won't load." Claude rewrote the whole file. It still wouldn't load. Nacho wrote "still the same" and Claude rewrote it again, now with a different structure. Three rounds and forty minutes later, the cause was the same one from the start. A file called styles.css that Nacho had accidentally saved as styles.css.txt.

theory.title: Three symptoms, three families of causes
theory.text: From your seat, a bug always looks like one of these three. It's worth knowing which one you're dealing with before writing a single word. Blank screen: the browser never even got to paint the content. Something broke very early, almost always a typo in the code or a file that's not where it's expected. Red text on screen: scary as it looks, this is the best of the three. The bug is presenting itself with a name and a location, and your job is reduced to copying it correctly. Nothing happens: you press the button and there's no error and no result either. This is the hard one. Either the program ran and failed silently, or nobody actually wired that button to anything. The difference matters because the question you need to ask the AI changes in each case. With the blank screen you ask what broke before painting. With the red text you don't ask anything: you paste the message. With the mute one you ask where the current stops flowing.
theory.analogy: Think of a lamp that won't turn on. A blown bulb is visible at a glance (red). A tripped fuse plunges the whole house into darkness at once (blank). And a switch that was never actually wired to the lamp gives no signal at all (mute). It flips up and down just fine, and nothing happens.
theory.example: All three, exactly as they appear. "Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' (at app.js:1:1)" is a file that doesn't contain what it was supposed to. "Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener') at app.js:14:23" is a button the program looks for and can't find. And the mute one writes nothing anywhere: that's why you have to go hunt for it.

theory.title: The entire error message, not summarized, not rewritten
theory.text: The most expensive mistake in this lesson is describing the bug in your own words. "I'm getting something about a module" and "Uncaught ReferenceError: calcularTotal is not defined at cart.js:32:5" are nowhere near the same information. In the second one you have the exact name of what's missing, the file, and the line. With that, the AI usually gets it right on the first try. Copy it with your mouse, never type it by hand. One changed letter or a missed capital and you send it hunting for something that doesn't exist. Paste it in full, including the five or six lines below that look like garbage and start with "at." That's the trace: the path the program took before it crashed. The cause is often on the third line, not the first. If it's forty lines, send all forty; they take up far less room than you think and don't get in the way. And if you only have the bug in a phone screenshot, attach the image and also type the first line by hand. AIs read images fairly well, but they'll confuse a 1 with an l at the first opportunity.
theory.example: Elena sells handmade candles in Logrono. She wrote "it won't let me pay" and went three rounds with no progress. When she finally copied the full message, the AI answered in a single message. The message was "Access to fetch at 'https://api.stripe.com/v1/checkout' from origin 'http://localhost:3000' has been blocked by CORS policy." She was testing checkout from her own computer instead of from the published site, and it was never going to work there. Five minutes.

theory.title: Where the evidence lives: the browser console
theory.text: Almost no error message from a webpage shows up on the page itself: it shows up in the console, a hidden panel inside the browser. It's not the terminal, nothing to install, and you can't break anything at all just by looking at it. It opens with the F12 key on Windows, or Cmd + Alt + J on a Mac. You can also right-click any empty spot on the page and choose "Inspect." The screen splits in two and a panel with tabs appears on top; of all of them you only need two. "Console" is where messages pile up: the red ones are real errors, the yellow ones are warnings you can almost always ignore. "Network" is the list of everything the page requested over the internet. There you see in red whatever didn't arrive: an image, a font, a payment response. A detail that catches everyone the first time: the console only logs what happens while it's open. Open it first, then reload the page. Otherwise you'll be staring at an empty panel, convinced there's no error at all.
theory.analogy: It's an airplane's black box. It keeps recording the whole time, including the malfunction, except nobody's going to open it until something goes wrong.
theory.example: There's no F12 on your phone, and you won't be able to open the console. If the bug only happens on your phone, the practical move is to take a screenshot and attach it. Also tell the AI whether it's an iPhone with Safari or an Android with Chrome. Some bugs only show up on one of the two, and knowing that saves it half a search.

theory.title: The six-point report
theory.text: A good bug report has six boxes and takes two minutes to fill in. The first four: what you expected to happen; what you did exactly, clicks in order; what actually happened; and the literal message. The fifth: what changed since the last time it worked. The sixth: where it happens, meaning which browser, which device, and whether it's every time or one in five. Point five is the one most people skip, and it's the one that closes the case on its own most often. A program that worked fine at six and broke at seven broke because of something that happened in between. And you're the only one who knows that. Point six looks like decoration until the day you discover the bug only happens on your mom's iPhone. The first four seem obvious. But notice the difference between "the page won't load" and "I expected to see the schedule list, I opened index.html in Chrome, clicked Book appointment, and the screen went blank." Write the report even if the bug seems small and you can't be bothered. You'll find that often, by the time you reach point five, you already know what happened and don't even need to send it.
theory.analogy: It's what a doctor asks you in the ER. What's wrong, since when, what did you do beforehand, has it happened before, and does it hurt all the time or only when you move. None of those questions are curiosity: each one crosses off half the list of possible causes.
theory.example: Point five in practice, written by Nacho: "it worked until I asked you to add the time-slot selector, two messages ago." With just that one sentence, the AI stops looking at 90% of the project and goes straight to the thirty new lines.

theory.title: Diagnose before fixing, and one thing at a time
theory.text: The fastest way to turn a small bug into a disaster is letting the AI try fixes blind. It proposes a change, it doesn't work, you write "still the same" and it proposes another. By the fourth round you're carrying four unverified changes, and you no longer know which one broke what used to work. The order that changes the outcome is this: "don't touch anything yet, tell me the three most likely causes and how I tell them apart." A language model (the program behind ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) follows this pretty well when you forbid it from acting. It instantly goes from a rushed plumber to someone who thinks. Then, one change at a time, and you verify before continuing. Also set yourself a limit: three rounds with no progress means the chat is weighed down by failed attempts. What's needed is opening a new one with a handoff that includes what you've already ruled out. And before letting it rewrite anything big, save a copy of what you have. If you tell it "do it again from scratch" and the new version comes out worse, there's no button that brings the old one back.
theory.analogy: A mechanic who swaps the battery, the spark plugs, and the alternator all at once and then starts the car hasn't fixed anything. He's spent $400 and still doesn't know what was broken. If it happens again tomorrow, he starts from zero.
theory.example: The difference in a real case. Elena sent "the pay button doesn't do anything, don't change anything yet, tell me the three most likely causes." The AI gave her three, with percentages. Checking the first one — looking at the Network tab when she clicked — took fifteen seconds and closed the case.

tasks.title: Open the browser console and stop fearing it
tasks.where: In your browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari), with any page open
tasks.action: Open a page you use every day. Press the F12 key, up at the top right of the keyboard. On Mac, press Cmd + Alt + J. If nothing happens, right-click any empty spot on the page and choose "Inspect" from the menu that appears. The screen splits in two and in the new half you'll see a row of tabs: Elements, Console, Sources, Network... Click "Console." Now, with the panel already open, reload the page with F5 and watch what shows up. Don't touch anything, just look. To close it, F12 again.
tasks.expect: A panel taking up half the bottom or right side of the window. You'll see the word Console highlighted and, below it, lines of text. On a large site you'll see yellow warnings and probably some red errors. That's normal: the world's most famous websites have console errors every single day. Messages showing up means you're in the right place.
tasks.stuck: If F12 raises your volume or turns off your wifi, your laptop has the F keys remapped by default: try Fn + F12. In Safari you have to enable it first: Safari menu → Settings → Advanced → check "Show features for web developers." From there Cmd + Alt + C works. There's no console on mobile: you'll diagnose those bugs with screenshots.

tasks.title: Copy an entire error without retyping a single letter
tasks.where: In the console you just opened
tasks.action: Find a red line. If it has a small triangle on the left, click to expand it: several lines starting with "at" will appear below. Right-click the red message: in Chrome and Edge you get the option "Copy message." That puts it on your clipboard. If that option doesn't appear, drag your mouse from the first character of the message to the end of the last "at" line. Release and press Ctrl + C (Cmd + C on Mac). Paste it into an empty chat to see it in full before actually using it.
tasks.expect: A block of text between one and twenty lines. The first usually carries one of these words: Uncaught, TypeError, SyntaxError, ReferenceError, or Failed to load resource. At the end of some line you'll see something like "app.js:14:23," meaning file app.js, line 14, character 23. That little piece is worth more than everything else combined.
tasks.stuck: If pasting only gives you ">" or a blank line, you copied the input box instead of the message. Drag again starting right above the first red letter. If the console is completely empty, open it and reload with F5 without closing it, because it only records what happens while it's open.

tasks.title: Manufacture all three bugs on purpose to see them up close
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in a new chat, then in your browser
tasks.action: Paste the request below. You'll get back four chunks of code, each in its own gray box with a copy button at top right. Open Notepad (Windows) or TextEdit (Mac) and paste the first. Save it to your Desktop as test-ok.html. On Windows, in the "Type" dropdown choose "All Files," otherwise it'll save as test-ok.html.txt and won't open. On Mac, before saving, go to Format → Make Plain Text. Repeat for the other three. Then open them one by one by double-clicking, with the console open in each, and watch what happens.
tasks.prompt:
I want to learn to read errors. Give me a single-page HTML file, no external libraries, no internet connection needed, that has:
- a title "Bug test"
- a counter that starts at 0
- an "Add 1" button that adds 1 to the counter

Give me four full versions, one after another, each in its own code block with its filename above it:

1. test-ok.html — working perfectly.
2. test-blank.html — same, but with a typo in the first line of the script, the kind that leaves the page completely blank.
3. test-red.html — same, but calling a function that doesn't exist, so a red error fires in the console when you click the button.
4. test-mute.html — same, but with the button's name misspelled in the code, so clicking it does absolutely nothing and the console stays empty.

Below each version, write in two lines what exact message I'll see in the browser console and why. Don't explain how to fix them yet.
tasks.expect: test-ok opens a page with its working counter button. test-blank opens an empty, white page, and the console shows a red line with the word SyntaxError. test-red looks fine until you click the button: then a red line fires with ReferenceError and the name of what doesn't exist. test-mute looks perfect, the button sinks when clicked, the counter doesn't move, and the console stays just as empty. Those four behaviors are what you'll run into for the rest of your life.
tasks.stuck: If double-clicking opens Notepad instead of the browser, the file got saved as .txt. Rename it, removing the .txt from the end. Beforehand, turn on "File name extensions" in the View tab of Windows Explorer. If the AI gives you all four files but none of them fail, reply: "2, 3, and 4 need to actually fail, give them back to me with the bug inside."

tasks.title: Build your six-point report
tasks.where: In the AI app, in the chat where you're building your project
tasks.action: Take whatever bug you have right now, or the one from test-red.html if you don't have your own project yet. Copy the template below and fill in the six brackets before hitting send. It takes two minutes. Don't skip point 5 even if it seems irrelevant — it's exactly the one that closes the case most often.
tasks.prompt:
I have a bug in the project we're building. I'm giving you the full report. Don't rewrite the whole project.

1. WHAT I EXPECTED TO HAPPEN
[Example: clicking "Book appointment" should have opened the form with the three fields]

2. WHAT I DID EXACTLY, STEP BY STEP
[Example: I opened index.html in Chrome, scrolled to the bottom, and clicked "Book appointment"]

3. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED
[Example: the page stayed the same, nothing opened, the button doesn't even sink when clicked]

4. ERROR MESSAGE, COPIED IN FULL AND UNTOUCHED
[Paste everything red from the console here, including the lines starting with "at." If there's nothing, write: "the console is empty"]

5. WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE LAST TIME IT WORKED
[Example: it worked until I asked you to add the time-slot selector, two messages ago]

6. WHERE IT HAPPENS
[Example: Chrome on Windows 11, laptop. Haven't tried mobile. Happens every time, all five times I've tried]

Before touching anything, tell me in one sentence what you think the cause is and which file and line you're going to change. Change only that. If you need to see a file you don't have in front of you, ask me for it and I'll paste it.
tasks.expect: An answer that starts by naming a specific cause and a specific file, not "it could be several things." If it proposes touching just one spot and tells you how to check whether it worked, you're in good shape.
tasks.stuck: If it comes back with a list of ten generic causes, point 4 was probably empty or summarized in your own words. Go back to the console, copy the literal message, and send it alone, with nothing else around it: "the exact message is this: ..."

tasks.title: Forbid it from touching anything until it diagnoses
tasks.where: In the same chat, right after sending the report
tasks.action: If the AI has jumped straight to rewriting half your project instead of explaining what's happening, rein it in with the message below. It's the one that'll save you the most time in the whole lesson. Then run the checks it gives you, one by one, and report back the result of each before letting it change anything.
tasks.prompt:
Stop. Don't change a single line yet.

With the report I just gave you, I only want a diagnosis:

1. The three most likely causes of this bug, ordered from most to least likely, with an approximate percentage for each.
2. For each cause, a check I can do myself in under a minute that tells me whether it's that one or not. I've never coded: tell me exactly where to click, don't give me code to write.
3. What information you're missing to be sure. If you need to see the content of one of my files, tell me its exact name and I'll paste it in the next message.

Don't give me the fix in this response. Just the diagnosis and the checks.
tasks.expect: Three causes with percentages (something like 60% / 25% / 15%) and three checks you can do with clicks. A good check sounds like: "open the Network tab, reload the page, and tell me if the app.js line shows up in red."
tasks.stuck: If it still hands you the fix, repeat just this: "I told you not to give me the solution yet, just the three causes and the three checks." It works on the second try almost every time. If it gives you checks with code to type into the console, reply: "without writing anything, just looking."

tasks.title: Track down the bug that says nothing
tasks.where: In your browser with the console open, then in the AI app
tasks.action: With the page open and the panel on the "Network" tab, click the button that doesn't do anything. Notice whether a new line shows up in the list. Note down what you see, even if it's "nothing shows up." Switch to the "Console" tab and check whether anything appeared, even if it's yellow. With those two observations you can send the message below.
tasks.prompt:
The [EXACT NAME ON THE BUTTON] button doesn't do anything when clicked. No red error shows up.

Here's what I see:
- Browser console: [paste whatever's there, even yellow warnings. If it's empty, say so]
- Network tab: when I click the button [a new line appears / no new line appears]. If it appears, it says: [paste the name and the number from the Status column]

Guide me through figuring out which of these three spots is broken:
a) the button isn't wired to anything
b) it is wired and the function starts, but it breaks partway through
c) the function runs to completion but nothing changes on screen

To tell them apart, give me the exact text I need to paste, in which file and which line, so a message of mine shows up in the console at each point along the way. Number the messages (1, 2, 3) so I know how far it got. Also tell me how to remove them afterward.
tasks.expect: The AI will give you one or two lines to paste in specific spots in the file. Those lines make a message appear in the console when the program passes through there. Reloading and clicking the button, you'll see in the console which messages come through and where it stops. That point is your bug.
tasks.stuck: If none of your messages show up, not even number 1, the button isn't wired to anything. Tell it exactly that and have it check how the button connects to the function. If all of them show up, all the way to the last one, the bug is in how the result gets painted on screen, not in the calculation. Tell it that too, since it changes where it needs to look.

tasks.title: Read the numbers: 404, 401, 403, 429, and 500
tasks.action: With the "Network" tab open, reload the page with F5. A table appears with one row for everything the page requested. Look at the "Status" column. Numbers starting with 2 are fine. Ones starting with 4 mean the fault is on your side. 404 is "what you're asking for doesn't exist here." 401 is "you haven't told me who you are." 403 is "I know who you are but you don't have permission." 429 is "you're asking for too many things in a row, slow down." Ones starting with 5 mean the problem is on the other computer and you can't fix it. Click any red row for details.
tasks.prompt:
In my browser's Network tab, this line shows up in red:
- Name: [PASTE THE FILE NAME OR ADDRESS]
- Status: [PASTE THE NUMBER, E.G. 404]
- Detail: [PASTE WHATEVER SHOWS UP WHEN YOU CLICK ON IT, IF ANYTHING]

Answer me three things, in this order, in plain terms:
1. Is the problem on my side or on the outside service's? Say it clearly in the first sentence.
2. If it's mine, what's the first check I should do, with clicks and no code to write.
3. If it's the outside service's, how do I check if it's down and what can I do meanwhile.

Don't rewrite anything from the project in this response.
tasks.expect: A table with columns Name, Status, Type, Size, and Time. If your page is working fine, you'll see everything at 200 and 304. If something's not loading, you'll see its name in red with a 404 next to it. That name is telling you exactly which file is missing or misnamed.
tasks.stuck: If the Network tab is empty, you opened it after the page loaded: leave it open and press F5. If you see a 429 on an AI service, that's not your fault. You've used up the number of requests your plan allows in that window. It's fixed by waiting or upgrading your plan (paid plans run around $20/month). If the number you see isn't on this list, paste it to the AI with "whose fault is it, mine or the service's?"

tasks.title: Save the working point before touching anything
tasks.where: In your computer's file explorer, in the project folder
tasks.action: Before accepting any big rewrite, go to your project folder. Right-click it, "Copy," right-click an empty spot next to it, "Paste." Rename the copy with the date and a word that identifies it: "booking-2026-08-19-working." If your project is a single file, copy the file. If you're working inside a Claude artifact or a ChatGPT Canvas and have nothing saved on your computer, do this: select all the code, copy it, and paste it into a separate document. Do it now, not the day you need it.
tasks.expect: Two folders (or two files) where there used to be one, with different names and one of them dated today. Open it and check that it really works. A copy you haven't opened isn't a backup, it's a folder with a nice name.
tasks.stuck: If you're working inside the chat and have no files on your computer, ask for it this way and save them. "give me the complete project, all the files, in separate code blocks with their names on top." Serious warning: if you say "rewrite it from scratch" without having saved a copy, the old version doesn't come back. The chat can be re-read, sure, but rescuing the good part out of forty messages is a lost afternoon.

tasks.title: Cut the loop after three rounds with no progress
tasks.where: In the AI app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Count the rounds. If you've had three proposed changes and the bug is exactly the same, don't send a fourth "still not working." Open a new chat with the "New chat" button (top left). Paste the handoff below, with the three failed attempts written out one by one. What you've ruled out is worth as much as what you've discovered, and in the old chat it's buried under twenty messages.
tasks.prompt:
Let's start fresh on this bug, because I've had three attempts with no progress.

CONTEXT
- What I'm building: [one sentence]
- What it's built with: [example: a single HTML file with its styling and JavaScript inside, nothing installed]
- Last version that worked: [example: yesterday afternoon's, before adding the form]

THE BUG
[paste your full six-point report here]

WHAT WE'VE ALREADY TRIED AND DIDN'T WORK
1. [change 1] → result: [exactly what happened]
2. [change 2] → result: [exactly what happened]
3. [change 3] → result: [exactly what happened]

RULES
- Don't repeat any of those three attempts.
- Start by telling me what those three results rule out.
- One change at a time, in one file only, and tell me how to check whether it worked before continuing.
tasks.expect: A first answer that starts by explaining what your three attempts rule out and that points somewhere different from where you'd been looking. If it proposes attempt number 1 again, it didn't read the list: repeat just that part, nothing else.
tasks.stuck: If you can't reconstruct the three attempts, ask this in the old chat: "summarize in a list what we've changed in this conversation and what result each change gave, without proposing anything new." Copy that list and use it for the handoff.

tasks.title: Write the bug's card so you don't repeat it
tasks.where: In the chat where you just fixed it, then in your notes
tasks.action: As soon as something gets fixed, and before building anything else, ask for the card with the message below. Paste it into a document called "Bugs and fixes" that has nothing else in it. In a month you'll have twelve cards, and you'll be surprised how often the new bug is a close cousin of an old one.
tasks.prompt:
The bug is fixed now. Write me the card for this case in exactly this format and nothing else:

SYMPTOM: [what I saw on screen, one line]
MESSAGE: [the literal error, exactly as it showed in the console. If there wasn't one, write "none"]
REAL CAUSE: [what was actually happening, in plain terms, one or two lines, no jargon]
FIX: [what changed and in which file]
FOR NEXT TIME: [one concrete rule that prevents this from happening to me again]

Maximum 120 words total. No intro, no closing, and no explaining the theory to me.
tasks.expect: Five short lines: symptom, message, real cause, fix, and rule for next time. No intro and no "hope this helps." You should be able to read it at a glance three months from now and understand it.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you a long text full of technical explanations, reply: "too long and too technical, maximum 120 words, write it for someone who has never coded." If it doesn't remember exactly what changed, tell it "review this whole conversation before writing the card."

matters: The literal message, in full, copied with your mouse. Summarizing it in your own words or typing it by hand turns a five-minute bug into a whole afternoon. The AI ends up hunting for a name that doesn't exist and rewrites healthy files along the way.

Point five of the report: what changed since the last time it worked. It's the line most people skip, and the one that closes the most cases on its own. It narrows the search from the entire project down to the thirty seconds when it broke.

One change at a time, verified before continuing. If you accept four changes in a row without checking any of them, when something works you won't know why, and when something breaks you won't either. You'll have lost the only information you had.

Saving a copy before any big rewrite. This one's irreversible: if you say "do it again from scratch" and the new version comes out worse, there's no undo button. Rescuing the good code out of a forty-message chat takes an entire afternoon.
ignore: Understanding what every word in the error message means. You don't need to, and you won't need to: your job is to copy it in full and put it in the right place. Translating it is exactly the AI's job, and it does it very well.
The console's yellow warnings. Almost all of them are minor complaints from third-party pieces and show up on your bank's website too. As long as there's nothing red, keep going.

The "Sources" tab, full of code, where you can freeze the program mid-run. It's a great tool for someone who codes daily. You get to the same place by asking the AI for the numbered messages from task 6, in a tenth of the time.
canDo: Read a literal error message and tell you which file and which line the problem is in. Often it doesn't even need to see the rest of the project.
Fix typos in one go: a misnamed variable, a missing comma, unclosed quotes. These are most of what you'll run into.
Give you a list of checks ordered by likelihood, with concrete clicks and no code to write, if you forbid it from giving you the fix before diagnosing.
Translate any error for you, no matter how cryptic it looks, and explain what it means for your case. That way you don't have to dig through forums in another language.
cantDo: See your screen, your folder, or your connection. If you don't tell it, as far as it's concerned it never happened.

Know what state your file is in right now. It remembers what it wrote, not what you saved, renamed, or changed by hand afterward. That's why it sometimes "fixes" code that's no longer what you actually have.
Repair what's out of your reach. For example: a service that's down, your monthly quota used up, a permission only the account owner can grant. It can recognize it and tell you, but it can't fix it.
Get it right without evidence. With "still not working" and nothing else, it's going to guess. And guessing three times in a row leaves the project worse than the original bug did.
words: A hidden panel inside the browser where the page logs everything that happens to it, including failures. Opens with F12, and you break nothing just by looking.
The lines that show up under a failure and start with "at." They're the path the program took before it broke, listed from the crash point backward.
A typo in the instructions: an extra comma, an unclosed parenthesis. The computer understands nothing and stops before it even starts, which is why it leaves you with a blank screen.
The list of everything your page requested over the internet while loading, marked with whether it arrived or not. It sits right next to the Console.
"What you asked for isn't here." Almost always means a misspelled name or something you moved to a different folder.
"You're asking for too many things too fast, wait a moment." Shows up when you use up the number of requests your plan allows.
The copy the browser keeps of a page so it opens faster next time. Sometimes it shows you the old version and makes you think your fix did nothing.
Finding the exact cause of a bug and removing it. It's not redoing everything: it's finding the specific broken piece and touching only that.
